name: Glow Protocol
lead: Glow Protocol, also sold as the GLOW blend, is a vendor-assembled peptide blend marketed online for skin quality. The usual listing combines GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 in one vial, with GHK-Cu making up most of the contents.[1][2] People take an interest in it hoping for a firmer, brighter, lit-from-within complexion and faster recovery after skin or tissue stress, drawing on GHK-Cu's association with collagen and wound-repair research.[1][3]

GHK-Cu is a copper-binding tripeptide isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart in the 1970s; laboratory work reported that it boosted collagen production in skin fibroblasts, and it appears in cosmetic anti-aging and hair products as copper tripeptide-1.[3] BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid peptide described in 1993 by Predrag Sikiric and studied mainly in animals for tendon, gut and wound healing.[4] TB-500 is a synthetic peptide based on an active region of thymosin beta-4, a protein that has been tested in phase 2 wound-healing trials.[5]

Vendors label the blend research use only, and RESIDENT magazine reports that a typical vial combines about 50 mg of GHK-Cu with 10 mg each of BPC-157 and TB-500, sold as freeze-dried laboratory material rather than a formulated serum.[1][2] Research on the individual peptides is mostly in cells and animals, and no published human study has tested the three-peptide combination.[1] Online interest has grown through video platforms and wellness forums, where before-and-after images and phrases such as "lit-from-within" are common in promotion.[1]

chain: GHK-Cu studied for collagen and wound repair; BPC-157 and TB-500 for tissue healing
Users expect better skin recovery and firmness
angle.text: People are drawn to the blend for a firmer, brighter complexion. The reasoning rests on GHK-Cu's collagen research and on repair studies of the other two peptides.

infobox: Sold as research use only; not approved as a drug or cosmetic[1]

paras: Most listings describe a vial dominated by GHK-Cu with smaller amounts of BPC-157 and TB-500, around 70 mg in total.[1][2] Some sellers list variants that add other peptides such as KPV, and contents differ between sellers.[2]

GHK-Cu: a copper-binding tripeptide (glycyl-histidyl-lysine) isolated from human plasma albumin by Loren Pickart in 1973 and identified in 1977. Wikipedia reports plasma levels of about 200 ng/ml at age 20 falling to about 80 ng/ml by age 60. Laboratory work from the late 1980s found that picomolar to nanomolar concentrations stimulated collagen synthesis in skin fibroblasts, and rat dermal wounds showed increases in protein, glycosaminoglycans and decorin. Rabbit, rat, mouse and pig wound studies reported better wound contraction, faster granulation tissue and improved blood vessel growth, and an ischemic rat flap study reported wound size falling 64.5 percent with GHK versus 45.6 percent with vehicle. Controlled facial studies reported firming and anti-wrinkle effects but had relatively small samples and short durations. It is widely used in cosmetic anti-aging and hair products under the INCI name copper tripeptide-1.[3] A 2018 review by Pickart and Margolina reported gene-expression data suggesting effects on many genes involved in tissue repair.[1]

BPC-157: a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide derived from a protein in human gastric juice, discovered and published on by Predrag Sikiric of the University of Zagreb in 1993, also called Body Protection Compound 157 or bepecin. Animal studies suggest cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, including on rat tendon and ligament healing, while human evidence is described as scarce: a retrospective study of 12 patients with knee pain, a pilot study on interstitial cystitis and a phase I trial whose results were not submitted. Its skin research is limited to rodent wound and burn models.[1][4]

TB-500: a synthetic version of an active region of thymosin beta-4, a natural protein involved in cell movement and tissue repair. The full protein sped healing of pressure ulcers, venous ulcers and epidermolysis bullosa in phase 2 trials and was reported safe and well tolerated there; animal studies of the peptide report effects on wound closure and blood vessel formation.[1][5]

The blend is not approved by the FDA as a drug or cosmetic.[1] An FDA advisory committee reviewed BPC-157 and TB-500 in July 2026 on whether licensed pharmacies may compound them, and FDA staff noted limited quality, safety and effectiveness data for BPC-157.[1] The World Anti-Doping Agency bans BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4.[4][5] Wikipedia also reports concern among researchers that BPC-157's promotion of new blood vessel growth could in theory affect tumour growth, and that health authorities discourage use because human safety data is insufficient.[4] Wikipedia reports that on 30 October 2026 the US health secretary announced that compounding pharmacies would be permitted to supply BPC-157 and several other peptides for human use despite the absence of FDA approval; it also states that BPC-157 is controlled as a prescription medicine in jurisdictions including Australia and New Zealand even though it is not marketed.[4]

RESIDENT magazine notes that research-grade peptides are raw materials not formulated or tested for skin application, and that buyers in the research field expect certificates of analysis with HPLC purity and mass-spectrometry identity confirmation. It describes before-and-after marketing as a red flag and the blend as sold for qualified laboratory study only.[1]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and online communities
paras: The blend is promoted through video platforms, social media and wellness forums under the name glow, with posts describing tighter skin, faster recovery and a lit-from-within look. RESIDENT reports that these posts rarely mention that vials are sold for laboratory research, and that the plausible mechanism for each peptide is not the same as evidence for the combination.[1] How individual people use such blends is not described here.

No studies found of the three-peptide blend. Research on GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 individually is mostly in cells and animals and concerns healing after injury; small facial studies of GHK-Cu and phase 2 wound trials of thymosin beta-4 are described above.[1][3][5]

timeline.event: Loren Pickart isolates GHK-Cu from human plasma albumin.[3]
FDA advisory committee reviews BPC-157 and TB-500 on pharmacy compounding.[1]

card.summary: A vendor blend of GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 that people use hoping for firmer, brighter-looking skin.
card.note: Sold as research use only; not FDA-approved; contents vary by vendor.

quick.overview:
Glow Protocol is an online peptide blend, usually GHK-Cu plus BPC-157 and TB-500, marketed for skin glow and recovery.

Users look to it for firmer, brighter skin, citing GHK-Cu's collagen research.
quick.mechanism: GHK-Cu is studied for collagen and wound repair; BPC-157 and TB-500 for tissue repair in animals. The combination itself has not been studied in people.
quick.risks: Sold as research use only and not approved as a drug or cosmetic. Contents and purity vary by vendor, and FDA staff have noted limited safety data for BPC-157.
